Cutting LLM Evaluation Costs with SySRs :
A Bandit Algorithm that Provably Exploits Model Similarity

Zifan Lyu1  Chahine Nejma2,3  Tobias Wegel1  Fanny Yang1  Florian E. Dorner1,4
1ETH Zurich  2Centrale Supélec  3ENS de Cachan  4MPI for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen
Correspondence to: zifan.lyu@inf.ethz.ch florian.dorner@tuebingen.mpg.de
Abstract

Large Language Models are typically benchmarked by evaluating every model on every test query. For practitioners seeking the best model to deploy, this is often wasteful: if a model clearly performs worse than others, there is no need to precisely estimate its performance. Best-arm identification algorithms can be naturally applied to drastically reduce costs by adaptively allocating evaluation budget. Further, language models often respond similarly to the same prompt—a property previous work has tried to leverage with mixed success. We propose Synchronized Successive Rejects (SySRs), augmenting the classical Successive Rejects algorithm with paired comparisons. Unlike prior attempts to leverage model similarity in best-model identification, our approach is hyperparameter-free and enjoys performance guarantees that improve with the degree of similarity between evaluated models. Empirically, our method outperforms all baselines in terms of average error rate across 15 standard benchmarks, and in terms of worst-case budget for reliably identifying the best model.

00footnotetext: Code available at llm-bandits-sysrs.

1 Introduction

As Large Language Models become more and more capable, evaluating and comparing their capabilities becomes increasingly pressing and expensive. With models able to reliably solve a growing number of relevant real-world tasks, the question which model to deploy is more relevant than ever. At the same time, the costs of answering this question are at an all-time high: Test-time scaling and agent loops cause surging inference costs, while mounting task complexity increases the cost of gold standard evaluations of models’ solutions. In particular, the labeling effort for generative tasks is much greater compared to earlier classification tasks, which could be evaluated by matching all models’ outputs to fixed ground-truth labels. For example, modern benchmark tasks like theorem proving or software development require independent evaluation of every single model’s response to a query, greatly increasing annotation costs.

Attempts to reduce evaluation costs include replacing expert annotators with Large Language Models (Zheng et al., 2023) or focusing evaluation on a smaller, pre-selected set of particularly informative subtasks (Maia Polo et al., 2024). Unfortunately, both approaches lack reliability and can produce severely misleading evaluation scores and model rankings (Bavaresco et al., 2025; Dorner et al., 2025; Yauney et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025). Focusing on model selection, Zhou et al. (2025) propose an orthogonal angle with strong statistical guarantees. They treat model evaluation as a multi-armed bandit problem in which models represent arms and per-query accuracy is the reward. Instead of fully evaluating all models, best-arm algorithms such as UCB-E can then decide which model to evaluate in an online fashion. Importantly, if some models turn out to be clearly worse than others, the algorithm can discard them early on, and instead focus on distinguishing between the best models. Indeed, Zhou et al. (2025) demonstrate that these algorithms can starkly reduce the cost of model selection.

While the theoretical properties of generic best-arm identification are well-understood (Audibert et al., 2010; Kaufmann et al., 2016; Ariu et al., 2021; Qin, 2022), the LLM benchmarking setting offers more structure than what is usually considered in the theoretical literature. In particular, across tasks, models’ performances are often highly correlated (Mania et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2025): Particularly easy tasks will be solved by the majority of models, while most models will fail to solve particularly hard tasks. Efficient evaluation algorithms should take this model similarity into account. However, the literature on multi-armed bandits with correlated arms is scarce. While Gupta et al. (2021b) discuss the best-arm identification setting, their approach is not directly applicable to LLM evaluation as it requires prior knowledge about the specific degree of correlation strength. Specific to LLM evaluation, Zhou et al. (2025) also proposed UCB-E-LRF – a variant of the UCB-E algorithm (Audibert et al., 2010) that uses low-rank factorization to predict model performance on unobserved evaluation cases. However, their approach comes without theoretical guarantees and does not consistently outperform standard UCB-E.

Contributions.

In this work, we propose a novel algorithm called Synchronized Successive Rejects (SySRs), based on the classical Successive Rejects algorithm (Audibert et al., 2010). Successive Rejects proceeds in stages: at each stage, it estimates each remaining arm’s performance and eliminates the worst-performing one. SySRs exploits the additional structure of benchmarks compared to the classical bandit setting via synchronization: Rather than independently sampling test queries for each model, each stage of SySRs samples a subset of test queries and evaluates all remaining models on the same set. We prove statistical performance guarantees for SySRs that scale with the correlation between evaluated models. Empirically, we find that averaged over 15 standard LLM benchmarks, SySRs outperforms all algorithms from prior work, including Zhou et al. (2025) (see Figure 1a). In addition, the performance of SySRs is highly consistent: As shown in Figure 1b), it reliably identifies the best model on all 15 benchmarks using at most 35% of the respective model/test-point pairs, while all other methods require more data on at least one benchmark to achieve the same. In short, our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce a novel correlation-aware best-arm identification algorithm called Synchronized Successive Rejects (SySRs) (Section 4).

  • •

    We prove an upper bound on the error rate of SySRs using a novel hardness measure that improves with between-model correlation (Section 5).

  • •

    We run extensive experiments on 15 standard LLM benchmarks, demonstrating SySRs’s strong performance compared to existing algorithms (Section 6).

2 Related Work

Efficient LLM Evaluation.

Perhaps the most common approach to reducing annotation costs in LLM evaluation is to replace expert annotators with so-called LLM judges (Zheng et al., 2023). While this approach can greatly reduce annotation costs and often works well, it has no bearing on inference costs and lacks reliability (Dorner et al., 2025; Bavaresco et al., 2025) when applied naïvely. One explanation for these reliability issues is model similarity (Mania et al., 2019) such as correlated error patterns between different models (Kim et al., 2025): A judge model that is too similar to the model it is supposed to evaluate might be unable to identify the latter’s mistakes (Goel et al., 2025).

While model similarity undermines LLM judges, more recent works aim to instead explicitly make use of it. Specifically, they aim to exploit similarity to construct smaller test sets that remain predictive of overall model performance (Vivek et al., 2024; Maia Polo et al., 2024). By reducing the amount of evaluated data points, these subset selection methods cut down on both annotation and inference costs. However, they lack theoretical guarantees and do not reliably outperform random subsampling test sets (Yauney et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025). Moreover, subset selection requires access to large amounts of historical evaluation data on a given benchmark to obtain the downsized test set. In contrast, our proposed SySRs algorithm can be applied to any benchmark, including novel ones with no historical data. In fact, SySRs is complementary to subset selection: whenever evaluation on a smaller test set is known to provide reliable information about overall benchmark performance, our approach can be applied to the subset to further speed up model selection.

Best-Model Identification.

While benchmark scores are often framed as absolute measurements of model capabilities (Sühr et al., 2026), they are highly sensitive to seemingly irrelevant details like prompt wording (Sclar et al., 2024) or the precise degree of data cleaning (Recht et al., 2019). Meanwhile, model rankings—describing which models outperform others—are surprisingly stable across contexts (Miller et al., 2021; Ruan et al., 2024), granting them a larger degree of external validity (Hardt, 2026). As such, we believe that often the appropriate goal for efficient LLM evaluation is to accurately rank models rather than precisely estimate model performance. Among potential ranking objectives, we focus on top-1 identification (that is, identifying the best model), which is arguably the most relevant for practice as it directly maps to deployment decisions.

Zhou et al. (2025) recognized that top-1 identification maps to the best-arm identification or pure exploration setting from the multi-armed bandit literature, and suggested using the popular UCB-E algorithm for model selection. While general best-arm identification is widely studied (Bubeck et al., 2009; Audibert et al., 2010; Kaufmann et al., 2016; Ariu et al., 2021), there is limited prior work on multi-armed bandits with correlated arms. Most relevantly, Gupta et al. (2020); Gupta et al. (2021a); Gupta et al. (2021b) study regret minimization and best-arm identification, modeling between-arm correlation as a known upper bound on one arm’s expected reward conditioned on observing another arm’s reward. However, in many cases no such nontrivial upper bound might be known a priori, despite between-arm correlation.

Specific to the LLM evaluation setting, Zhou et al. (2025) also propose to exploit between-model correlation by combining UCB-E with low-rank factorization to predict LLM scores on unseen queries. However, their method does not come with any theoretical performance guarantees and underperforms UCB-E in our experiments. In contrast, our SySRs algorithm outperforms UCB-E on average and comes with theoretical guarantees that scale with the degree of correlation between models, while not requiring a priori knowledge about that degree.

3 Formal Setup and Existing Algorithms

We consider the problem of identifying the best model among a set of KK candidate Large Language Models (LLMs) f1,…,fKf_{1},\dots,f_{K} on a given test set 𝒳={x1,…,xL}\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{L}\}, using a fixed finite testing budget of nn evaluations. For each prompt xi∈𝒳x_{i}\in\mathcal{X}, we denote the performance of model fjf_{j} on xix_{i} as Si​jS_{ij}. As both the model’s answer and the scoring can be non-deterministic, we model Si​jS_{ij} to be independently drawn from a distribution ϕi​j\phi_{ij} with bounded support in [0,1][0,1]. The stochastic performance matrix 𝐒=(Si​j)i​j∈[0,1]K×L\mathbf{S}=(S_{ij})_{ij}\in[0,1]^{K\times L} then generalizes the deterministic performance matrix from Zhou et al. (2025).

Following Zhou et al. (2025), we view adaptive LLM evaluation as revealing entries of the unknown matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, but allow these entries to be stochastic. In particular, we consider (potentially randomized) algorithms that operate in nn steps, and at each step t∈{1,…,n}t\in\{1,\dots,n\}

  1. 1.

    Select a model index it∈{1,…,K}i_{t}\in\{1,\dots,K\} and a test instance index jt∈{1,…,L}j_{t}\in\{1,\dots,L\}.

  2. 2.

    Observe the score Sit​jtS_{i_{t}j_{t}}.

The goal of the algorithm is to identify the model fif_{i}, or “arm”, with the largest average performance, defined as

i⋆∈arg⁡maxi∈{1,…,K}⁡μiwhereμi:=1L​∑j=1L𝔼Si​j∼ϕi​j​[Si​j].i^{\star}\in\arg\max_{i\in\{1,\dots,K\}}\mu_{i}\quad\text{where}\quad\mu_{i}:=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{S_{ij}\sim\phi_{ij}}[S_{ij}].

After nn steps, the algorithm produces a guess I^\widehat{I} for the best arm i⋆i^{\star}, and we measure an algorithm’s performance in terms of its error probability en=ℙ⁡(I^≠i⋆)e_{n}=\mathbb{P}(\widehat{I}\neq i^{\star}). This probability is defined over both the noisy model responses and the algorithm’s internal randomness, which determines the sequence of queried model-prompt pairs.

Standard best-arm identification algorithms with fixed budget can straightforwardly be applied to this setting by viewing μi\mu_{i} as the expectation 𝔼[Ri]\EE[R_{i}] of the reward Ri=Si​JR_{i}=S_{iJ}, where a test set index JJ is drawn uniformly from {1,…,L}\{1,\dots,L\}. However, the matrix formulation allows us to additionally capture the correlation structure between models. Formally, indices JJ sampled uniformly from {1,…,L}\{1,\dots,L\} induce random vectors (R1,…,RK)=(S1​J,…,SK​J)(R_{1},...,R_{K})=(S_{1J},...,S_{KJ}) with the desired expectation (μ1,…,μK)(\mu_{1},...,\mu_{K}) and potentially non-trivial correlation structure. This contrasts with standard multi-armed bandit settings, where independence is typically assumed both across arms and tasks.

3.1 Best-arm Identification Algorithms

In this section, we present how to use two classical and one tailored best-arm identification algorithms for LLM evaluation. The Successive Rejects algorithm (SR), first introduced by Audibert et al. (2010), addresses the problem of finding the best-performing model by dividing the evaluation budget nn into K−1K-1 phases and progressively eliminating models. The lengths of each phase follow a carefully designed hyperparameter-free schedule. Within each phase, all models in the active set are tested equally often by selecting one test instance for each model independently and uniformly at random. At the end of each phase, the single worst-performing model (based on empirical mean) is removed from the set of remaining models. After the last phase, exactly one model remains, which is returned as I^SR\widehat{I}_{\operatorname{SR}}.

Audibert et al. (2010) also introduced the Upper Confidence Bound Exploration (UCB-E) algorithm, a variant of the classical UCB algorithm (Auer, 2002) that allows for the degree of exploration to be controlled by a hyperparameter aa. The algorithm selects models based on an exploration index: μ^i+a/si\hat{\mu}_{i}+\sqrt{a/s_{i}} where sis_{i} is the number of times the model ii has been queried. The algorithm runs for nn rounds, in each of which the model with the highest exploration index is evaluated by drawing a test instance independently and uniformly at random. After the last round, UCB-E returns the model I^UCB−E\widehat{I}_{\operatorname{UCB-E}} with the largest empirical mean.

As these classical algorithms do not make use of the given matrix structure, Zhou et al. (2025) propose two adaptations to the UCB-E tailored to the LLM evaluation setting: The first method is a simple modification of UCB-E that avoids evaluating the same model/query pair twice. Instead of sampling queries xj∈𝒳x_{j}\in\mathcal{X} with replacement, the algorithm keeps track of which entries xjx_{j} a model fif_{i} has already been evaluated on and ensures no model is evaluated twice on the same query. The second method called UCB-E-LRF is more involved. For deterministic scores Si​jS_{i}j the algorithm fits an ensemble of low-rank matrices 𝐒^\hat{\mathbf{S}} at each step, aiming to reconstruct the score matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S} from the limited already observed entries. It then selects both the model fif_{i} to evaluate and the query xjx_{j} to evaluate on, based on a combination of the observed entries, and both the mean and variance of the ensemble 𝐒^\hat{\mathbf{S}}. Both algorithms are described in detail in Sections C.1 and C.2.

3.2 Guarantees for Classical Best-Arm Identification

Classical algorithms for Best-Arm Identification come with strong guarantees on the error probability ene_{n}. The guarantees depend on a hardness measure that captures the difficulty of the problem. Since distinguishing between two almost equivalent models is harder than separating the best candidate from a low performer, hardness measures usually depend on the gap between the mean scores μi\mu_{i}.

Formally, standard hardness measures are usually defined by first reordering the models/arms ii in terms of decreasing mean so that μ(1)≥μ(2)≥⋯≥μ(K)\mu_{(1)}\geq\mu_{(2)}\geq\cdots\geq\mu_{(K)}. For i>1i>1, we then define the sub-optimality gaps

Δi=μ⋆−μ(i),whereμ⋆=maxi∈{1,…,K}⁡μi=μ(1)=μi⋆,\Delta_{i}=\mu^{\star}-\mu_{(i)},\quad\text{where}\quad\mu^{\star}=\max_{i\in{\{1,\dots,K\}}}\mu_{i}=\mu_{(1)}=\mu_{i^{\star}},

setting Δ1=Δ2\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{2} such that

Δ1=Δ2≤⋯≤ΔK.\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{2}\leq\dots\leq\Delta_{K}.

In the classical fixed-budget best-arm identification setting, the hardness of the problem instance is typically captured by the quantities H1H_{1} and H2H_{2}, defined by Audibert et al. (2010):

H1=∑i=1K1Δi2,H2=maxi∈{2,…,K}⁡iΔi2.H_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{K}\frac{1}{\Delta_{i}^{2}},\qquad H_{2}=\max_{i\in\{2,\dots,K\}}\frac{i}{\Delta_{i}^{2}}.

The two quantities are related by the inequalities

H2≤H1≤log⁡(2​K)​H2.H_{2}\leq H_{1}\leq\log(2K)\,H_{2}.

Assuming the exploration parameter aa for the UCB-E algorithm is chosen to satisfy 0<a≤2536​n−KH10<a\leq\frac{25}{36}\frac{n-K}{H_{1}}, Audibert et al. (2010) prove the following guarantee for UCB-E:

ℙ(I^UCB−E≠i⋆)\displaystyle\PP\left(\widehat{I}_{\operatorname{UCB-E}}\neq i^{\star}\right) ≤2​n​K​exp⁡(−2​a25),\displaystyle\leq 2nK\exp\left(-\frac{2a}{25}\right), (1)

which Zhou et al. (2025) show to remain valid for LLM evaluation with queries sampled without replacement, when the scores Si​jS_{ij} are deterministic. However, H1H_{1} is usually not known a priori, such that users face the difficult task of guessing the exploration parameter aa both small enough to achieve the guarantee and large enough to obtain a sufficiently small value in the exponential. Meanwhile, SR enjoys a similar guarantee (Audibert et al., 2010), without hyperparameters :

ℙ(I^SR≠i⋆)\displaystyle\PP\left(\widehat{I}_{\operatorname{SR}}\neq i^{\star}\right) ≤K⁡(K−1)2​exp⁡(−n−Klog¯​(K)​H2),\displaystyle\leq\frac{K(K-1)}{2}\exp\left(-\frac{n-K}{\overline{\log}(K)H_{2}}\right), (2)

where log¯​(K)=12+∑i=2K1i\overline{\log}(K)=\frac{1}{2}+\sum_{i=2}^{K}\frac{1}{i}. Unlike UCB-E-LRF, neither of the two algorithms attempt to take advantage of the correlation between arms, which is reflected in neither bound depending on said correlation. On the other hand, due to its relatively high complexity, there are no known performance bounds for UCB-E-LRF. In the next section, we propose a novel algorithm that comes with performance guarantees that improve with the correlation between evaluated models.

4 Synchronized Successive Rejects (SySRs)

In this section, we introduce the Synchronized Successive Rejects (SySRs) algorithm, inspired by Successive Rejects (SR). SR is particularly suited for adaptation to our setting for multiple reasons: First, one can easily modify it to utilize model correlation by evaluating different LLMs on the same test instances. Second, unlike UCB-style algorithms that involve switching models at every step, SR evaluates active models on blocks of test instances in every phase, allowing for straightforward batched LLM inference. Lastly, SR is hyperparameter free, allowing us to avoid parameter tuning and adapt to correlation without a priori knowledge of its strength. In particular, as we will demonstrate, adapting SR yields a clean theoretical analysis of the error probability that scales with the correlation strength.

Similar to SR, SySRs relies on a static allocation strategy. It splits the evaluation budget nn into K−1K-1 unequally sized phases (with KK the number of models). The phases are carefully scheduled such that the budget is efficiently utilized. In particular, for n>Kn>K, the budget assigned to each phase k=1,…,K−1k=1,\dots,K-1 is defined as nk−nk−1n_{k}-n_{k-1} per remaining model, where in turn nkn_{k} is defined as

nk=⌈1log¯​(K)​n−KK+1−k⌉,log¯​(K)=12+∑i=2K1i.n_{k}=\Big\lceil\frac{1}{\overline{\log}(K)}\frac{n-K}{K+1-k}\Big\rceil,\quad\overline{\log}(K)=\frac{1}{2}+\sum_{i=2}^{K}\frac{1}{i}. (3)

In phase kk, all K+1−kK+1-k remaining models are evaluated on the same subset 𝒥~k\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{k} of nk−nk−1n_{k}-n_{k-1} queries. We sample the evaluation queries 𝒥~k\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{k} uniformly at random, without replacement as Zhou et al. (2025) do for UCB-E to ensure we do not evaluate models on the same test instance more than once.

We then eliminate the worst model according to the empirical mean of rewards μ^i,nk=1nk​∑j∈𝒥kSi​j\widehat{\mu}_{i,n_{k}}=\frac{1}{n_{k}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{k}}S_{ij}, where 𝒥k=⋃t≤k𝒥~t\mathcal{J}_{k}=\bigcup_{t\leq k}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{t} is the set of queries the remaining models have been evaluated on. By design, after phase kk, each remaining model has been evaluated exactly nkn_{k} times. Moreover as verified by Audibert et al. (2010), the total budget spent does not exceed the allowed budget nn. We summarize this procedure in Algorithm 1.

Contrary to the classical SR algorithm, which samples rewards independently for each arm, SySRs explicitly exploits the correlation between different models by evaluating the entire set of remaining models on the same test instances in each phase. As with paired comparison tests, given between-model correlation, this allows for more precise estimates of the performance gap between two models. In the next section, we explain this in more detail and quantify the resulting gains from synchronization.

Theorem 5.1.

Let I^✂\widehat{I}_{\text{✂}} be the arm chosen by SySRs (Algorithm 1) with a budget of nn. The probability ene_{n} that I^✂\widehat{I}_{\text{✂}} is not the best arm i⋆i^{\star} is then upper bounded as follows:

en:=ℙ⁡(I^✂≠i⋆)≤K⁡(K−1)2​exp⁡(−n−Klog¯​(K)​H3),e_{n}:=\mathbb{P}(\widehat{I}_{\text{✂}}\neq i^{\star})\;\leq\;\frac{K(K-1)}{2}\exp\left(-\frac{n-K}{\overline{\log}(K)H_{3}}\right),

where H3H_{3} is the correlation-aware hardness quantity defined in Equation 4.

We prove Theorem 5.1 in appendix B. Our proof follows the classical SR analysis in Audibert et al. (2010). The key difference is that it uses a version of Bernstein’s inequality rather than Hoeffding’s inequality to bound the error rate for comparing the means of any pair of arms.

Intuitively, SySRs reduces error probability by the same mechanism a paired difference test improves compared to a two-sample test. At the end of a given phase kk, the probability of an error is upper bounded by the probability that the estimated gap μ^i⋆−μ^(i)\widehat{\mu}_{i^{\star}}-\widehat{\mu}_{(i)} is negative for any remaining model (i)(i). This probability in turn depends on the variance V⋆,iV_{\star,i} of the score difference Si⋆​j−S(i)​jS_{i^{\star}j}-S_{(i)j}. Formally, by the definition of H3H_{3} in Equation 5, the bound in Theorem 5.1 tightens whenever the variance V⋆,iV_{\star,i} is small. By exposing all models to the same test instances, we make use of between-model correlation to reduce that variance (Equation 6). As discussed in detail later, this tightening is particularly decisive in the ”hard” regime where the score gaps Δi\Delta_{i} are small and identifying the optimal arm requires the most samples.

5.1 Regimes Where Synchronization Pays Off

While Theorem 5.1 and Equation 2 share a similar structure, we highlight the gains in our result by discussing some sufficient conditions for our bound to be (much) smaller. We define θi∈[0,1]\theta_{i}\in[0,1] as the normalized correlation parameter between the best arm and the ii-th-ranked arm:

θi:=Cov⁡(Si⋆​J,S(i)​J)(μ⋆−Δi)​(1−μ⋆)\theta_{i}:=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(S_{i^{\star}J},S_{(i)J})}{(\mu^{\star}-\Delta_{i})(1-\mu^{\star})}

where (μ−Δ)​(1−μ)(\mu-\Delta)(1-\mu) is the maximum achievable covariance between two random variables in [0,1][0,1] with means μ\mu and μ−Δ\mu-\Delta respectively. We focus on the case of positive between-model correlation, in which we have that θi∈[0,1]\theta_{i}\in[0,1]. In Proposition A.1, we prove a detailed sufficient condition on (θi)i≠1(\theta_{i})_{i\neq 1} for H3H_{3} to be smaller than H2H_{2}. The threshold θ⋆\theta^{\star} derived there tightly characterizes the boundary for improvement. However, due to the algebraic complexity of this result, we distill the following corollary.

Corollary 5.2 (Simplified Sufficient Conditions).

If for every suboptimal arm, either

θi>2​ΔiorΔi<32​μ⋆−1,\theta_{i}>2\Delta_{i}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\Delta_{i}<\tfrac{3}{2}\mu^{\star}-1,

then the correlation-aware hardness satisfies H3<H2H_{3}<H_{2}.

Corollary 5.2 implies that H3H_{3} is commonly smaller than H2H_{2}, even when between-model correlation is modest. If all evaluated models have similar capabilities, all Δi\Delta_{i} are small such that small values of θi\theta_{i} already suffice for the first condition. Similarly, if the best model has high average score μ⋆≈1\mu^{\star}\approx 1 while all other models perform noticeably better than chance (μi≫0.5\mu_{i}\gg 0.5), the second condition is fulfilled even when there is no correlation.

We would like to highlight that the comparison of H2H_{2} and H3H_{3} relies on two separate mechanisms: a better suited analysis and an improved algorithm. Our analysis can equally be applied to standard SR, leading to an error bound where H3H_{3} is replaced by

H3′=maxi∈{2,…,K}⁡i​H3,i′,whereH3,i′=2​Var⁡(Si⋆​J)+2​Var⁡(S(i)​J)+23​(1+Δi)​ΔiΔi2\begin{split}H^{\prime}_{3}&=\max_{i\in\{2,\dots,K\}}iH^{\prime}_{3,i},\quad\text{where}\\ H^{\prime}_{3,i}&=\frac{2\operatorname{Var}(S_{i^{\star}J})+2\operatorname{Var}(S_{(i)J})+\frac{2}{3}(1+\Delta_{i})\Delta_{i}}{\Delta_{i}^{2}}\end{split}

uses the sum of per-arm variances rather than V⋆,iV_{\star,i}. In certain regimes (e.g., when the second condition of Corollary 5.2 holds), this will yield tighter performance bounds than Equation 2, even for standard SR. On the algorithmic side, SySRs improves performance by being able to leverage positive correlation between models. This is reflected in the scaling of H3H_{3} with the correlation strength θi\theta_{i}, while H3′H^{\prime}_{3} is unaffected by any between-arm correlation.

Averaging over the datasets summarized in Table 1, we indeed observe that usually H3<H3′<H2H_{3}<H^{\prime}_{3}<H_{2}. This shows that both tighter analysis and algorithmic improvements play an important role for our improved theoretical guarantees.

5.2 The Two-Armed Case

To build further intuition for the scaling of the correlation-aware hardness H3H_{3}, we focus on the simplified two-arm Bernoulli setting with means μ\mu and μ−Δ\mu-\Delta. We discuss how H3H_{3} scales with the performance gap Δ\Delta and correlation, and compare it to H2H_{2}. We consider a deterministic score matrix 𝐒∈{0,1}2×L\mathbf{S}\in\{0,1\}^{2\times L} with the normalized correlation parameter θ=CovJ∼Unif​(1,⋯,L)​(Si⋆​J,S(2)​J)/((μ−Δ)​(1−μ))\theta=\mathrm{Cov}_{J\sim\text{Unif}(1,\cdots,L)}(S_{i^{\star}J},S_{(2)J})/((\mu-\Delta)(1-\mu)).

In particular, we have the two following edge cases.

(i) Uncorrelated rewards (θ=0\theta=0). When arms are uncorrelated, the variance of the score difference equals the sum of the per-arm variances:

V⋆,2=Var⁡(Si⋆​J−S(2)​J)=Var⁡(Si⋆​J)+Var⁡(S(2)​J).V_{\star,2}\;=\;\operatorname{Var}(S_{i^{\star}J}-S_{(2)J})\;=\;\operatorname{Var}(S_{i^{\star}J})+\operatorname{Var}(S_{(2)J}). (7)

As a result, in this regime, H3=H3′=Θ⁡(1/Δ2)H_{3}=H^{\prime}_{3}=\Theta(1/\Delta^{2}) as Δ→0\Delta\to 0, recovering the classical hardness H2H_{2} up to constant factors.

(ii) Maximally correlated rewards (θ=1\theta=1). Under binary scores and deterministic per-instance scores, this case arises naturally from a point-wise dominant model (Mania and Sra, 2020), where the optimal model is necessarily correct whenever the suboptimal model is correct (S(2)​j=1⟹Si⋆​j=1S_{(2)j}=1\implies S_{i^{\star}j}=1). This structural dependence forces maximal correlation (θ=1\theta=1), leading to a simplified variance

V⋆,2=Δ−Δ2V_{\star,2}=\Delta-\Delta^{2} (8)

such that hardness scales as H3=Θ⁡(1/Δ)H_{3}=\Theta\left(1/\Delta\right) for Δ→0\Delta\to 0.

This improvement is reminiscent of fast rate phenomena in statistical learning theory. There, Bernstein-type conditions (Bartlett and Mendelson, 2006) control the variance of the excess loss by its expectation, allowing sample complexities to interpolate between the slow rate 1/ε21/\varepsilon^{2} and the fast rate 1/ε1/\varepsilon (Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, 2014, Appendix B.5). Here, Equation 8 yields an analogous relation:

Var⁡(Si⋆​J−S(2)​J)\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}(S_{i^{\star}J}-S_{(2)J}) ≤Δ=𝔼[Si⋆​J−S(2)​J].\displaystyle\leq\Delta=\EE[S_{i^{\star}J}-S_{(2)J}].

Thus the variance of the arm difference shrinks linearly with the gap, which explains why the correlation-aware hardness improves from the classical Θ⁡(1/Δ2)\Theta(1/\Delta^{2}) scaling to Θ⁡(1/Δ)\Theta(1/\Delta) in this maximally correlated regime. In this sense, Equation 8 plays the role of a Bernstein condition for the score differences.

A Matching Lower Bound.

To further motivate the hardness measure H3H_{3}, in appendix A we also prove the following lower bound: Consider the problem of identifying the better of two models with expected score gap Δ\Delta and variance of the score difference V⋆,2V_{\star,2}, using nn i.i.d. pairs of binary scores {(S1​ji,S2​ji)}i=1n\left\{(S_{1j_{i}},S_{2j_{i}})\right\}_{i=1}^{n} from the two models.

Theorem 5.3 (Informal version of Theorem A.2).

In the setting above, any algorithm returning I^\widehat{I} incurs error at least

en=ℙ(I^≠i⋆)≥c1​exp⁡(−c2​nH3)e_{n}=\PP(\widehat{I}\neq i^{\star})\geq c_{1}\exp\left(-c_{2}\frac{n}{H_{3}}\right)

on at least one distribution of (S1​J,S2​J)(S_{1J},S_{2J}) adhering to the gap and variance constraints. Here c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0 are two universal constants.

The formal version of this statement can be found in Theorem A.2. In particular in the 2-model i.i.d. setting, if all we know is that the variance equals V⋆,2V_{\star,2} and the gap equals Δ\Delta, then H3H_{3} measures the optimal sample complexity (in a minimax sense), which is achieved by SySRs up to constants. While a generalization to sampling without replacement is open and likely requires a finite sample correction similar to the Bernstein-Serfling inequality Bardenet and Maillard (2015), we expect this correction to be minor when the benchmark dataset size LL is large compared to the budget nn.

6 Experiments

Having established theoretical guarantees for SySRs, we now validate its performance empirically, comparing it to algorithms from previous work.

6.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets and Models.

We base our experiments on publicly available per-query results for 15 standard benchmark datasets, sourced from HELM Lite (Liang et al., 2023) and the OpenLLM Leaderboard (Beeching et al., 2023). For each benchmark, we include all models for which evaluation results were available for all queries in December 2025. As all considered benchmarks use greedy decoding, all scores Si​jS_{ij} are deterministic11 1 Note that this does not make the rewards Ri=Si​JR_{i}=S_{iJ} deterministic, as test set indices JJ are still randomized.. This is consistent with our theoretical model, as the special case in which the distributions ϕi​j\phi_{ij} are point masses.

Table 1 summarizes key statistics across all datasets, showing substantial variation in both dataset size and difficulty in terms of the hardness measures H2H_{2} and H3H_{3}. For more details on the datasets, see Table D.1 in the appendix.

Baselines.

We compare SySRs to the following baselines:

  • •

    Uniform Sampling (US) evaluates each model on equally many test instances, each independently drawn uniformly without replacement.

  • •

    Synchronized Uniform Sampling (SyUS) randomly selects test instances uniformly without replacement, evaluating all models on the same subset of instances.

  • •

    UCB-E from Audibert et al. (2010).

  • •

    UCB-E with low-rank factorization (UCB-E-LRF) from Zhou et al. (2025)

  • •

    Successive Rejects (SR) from Audibert et al. (2010).

  • •

    Synchronized UCB-E (SyUCB-E): a novel correlation-aware variant of UCB-E, using a global task schedule similar to SySRs (see Section C.3).

We run all (non-LRF) UCB-E variants for the exploration parameters a∈{0.1,1.0,10.0}a\in\{0.1,1.0,10.0\}. For UCB-E-LRF, we evaluate two variants: one with the default hyperparameters from Zhou et al. (2025) (including a warm-up phase consisting of 5% of the benchmark size K×LK\times L), and one with no warm-up phase, which we call UCB-E-LRF(No Warm-up).

All algorithms use sampling without replacement. We slightly modify all algorithms except for UCB-E-LRF to ensure well-defined behavior when a model has already been evaluated on the full set of queries 𝒳\mathcal{X}. UCB-E-LRF already handles this case natively. For the other UCB-E variants, we simply exclude fully evaluated models from the arm selection. For SR and SySRs, we modify the schedule, capping nkn_{k} at the number of queries in the test set LL and reallocating the freed-up budget proportionally to earlier phases. Additional implementation details for all algorithms can be found in appendix E.

Evaluation Metrics.

For each benchmark, we define the best-performing model i⋆i^{\star} as the one with the highest average performance across all test instances. As our primary evaluation metric, we measure the error probability en=ℙ⁡(I^≠i⋆)e_{n}=\mathbb{P}(\widehat{I}\neq i^{\star}), quantifying the likelihood that an algorithm fails to identify the best-performing model for a given evaluation budget nn. We call 1−en1-e_{n} the identification accuracy. To obtain robust empirical estimates e^n\hat{e}_{n} for ene_{n}, we perform 10001000 independent runs per algorithm. For UCB-E-LRF and UCB-E-LRF (No Warm-up), we reduce the number of runs to 100100 due to their high computational overhead. Each run uses a different random seed to sample the subset of queries used by the algorithms. We then estimate e^n\hat{e}_{n} as the fraction of runs in which the algorithm fails to identify the best model.

To enable comparison across datasets of different sizes, we express the budget as a percentage b=nKD×LDb=\frac{n}{K_{D}\times L_{D}} of the full evaluation budget, where KDK_{D} and LDL_{D} denote the number of models and test instances of dataset DD, respectively. We then estimate the error probability at regular intervals of budget percentage bb, denoting our estimates ϵ^b\hat{\epsilon}_{b}. Based on ϵ^b\hat{\epsilon}_{b}, we analyze the performance of algorithms in two ways that are comparable across datasets: First, as in Figure 1, we study how ϵ^b\hat{\epsilon}_{b} changes with the budget percentage bb. This provides us with insights into how well algorithms perform given a fixed percentage of the evaluation budget. Second, we define the X% Confidence Budget (CB) as the minimum budget percentage b⋆b^{\star} such that the empirical identification accuracy 1−ϵ^b1-\hat{\epsilon}_{b} satisfies 1−ϵ^b≥X%1-\hat{\epsilon}_{b}\geq X\% for all evaluated budget percentages b≥b⋆b\geq b^{\star}. In other words, identification accuracy stays above X%X\% once the budget percentage exceeds the X% CB. This dual view informs us how much evaluation budget an algorithm needs to achieve a target error rate.

6.2 Main Results

We now present the main experimental results, focusing on both the identification accuracy view and the confidence budget view across datasets. Both views confirm SySRs’ efficiency for model selection, as well as broader benefits of synchronization.

The Average Identification Accuracy View.

Table 2 shows the identification accuracy averaged across all 15 datasets at different budget percentages. Our hyperparameter-free SySRs outperforms all baselines for all tested hyperparameters at all considered budgets. In particular, at 12% of the budget, SySRs achieves an average identification accuracy of 95% while all other bandit methods stay below 90% and the uniform sampling baselines do not even reach 50%.

The results in Table 2 also demonstrate the impact of dataset synchronization, more broadly: For all of US, UCB-E, and SR, the synchronized variants outperform the non-synchronized version, often by around ten percentage points. In particular SyUCB-E, our synchronized version of UCB-E, gets close to SySRs’ performance at some budgets, but remains sensitive to hyperparameter choice. For more fine-grained results on identification error, including per-benchmark results, see Appendix F.

The Average and Worst-Case Confidence Budget View.

To complement the budget-averaged perspective, we analyze algorithm performance using the Confidence Budget (CB) defined in the previous section. Table 3 shows the mean and maximum of the CB across datasets for each algorithm at the 90%, 95%, and 100% identification accuracy levels. SySRs consistently achieves the lowest mean and maximum CB values across all three accuracy thresholds, indicating its superior efficiency in identifying the best model with high confidence. In particular, across all datasets, SySRs needs to evaluate at most 35% of model/query pairs to identify the best model with probability one. Meanwhile, SR requires 43%, the best UCB variants need around 50%, and the non-bandit baselines essentially require the full evaluation budget to achieve the same.

As before, we observe that synchronized algorithms (SySRs, SyUCB-E and SyUS) outperform their non-synchronized counterparts (SR, UCB-E and US respectively) in almost all cases. This highlights the consistent benefits of leveraging model similarity through synchronized task selection.

Beyond this, Table 3 starkly illustrates the dependence of UCB-E variants on hyperparameter selection. While SR and SySRs perform well without any hyperparameters, the performance of UCB-E and SyUCB-E is strongly affected by the exploration parameter aa. Although lower values of aa (e.g., a=1.0a=1.0) tend to perform much better in terms of the 90% CB, higher values (e.g., a=10.0a=10.0) are needed to identify the best model with perfect reliability (i.e., to achieve strong performance in terms of 100% CB). Again, more fine-grained results can be found in Appendix F.

Additional Experiments.

Going beyond best model identification, appendix H provides preliminary experiments on using SySRs and other bandit algorithms for top-mm model identification and other model ranking tasks. We find that bandit algorithms continue to perform much better than uniform sampling. SySRs performs particularly well in terms of worst-case performance, and for small mm, but SyUCB-E has an edge in terms of average error rates, especially when mm gets larger. In addition, appendix G compares our approach to subset selection methods (Vivek et al., 2024; Maia Polo et al., 2024), which aim to construct smaller but predictive test sets (see Section 2). As suggested by prior work (Zhang et al., 2025; Yauney et al., 2026), these methods mostly bring minor improvements over uniform sampling, and evaluation on the resulting test sets yields much higher identification error rates than using SySRs.

7 Limitations and Future Work

Our first guarantees on gains from model similarity in LLM selection open up multiple avenues for future research. First, we observe that despite the strong average performance of SySRs across datasets, UCB algorithms can outperform SySRs for some combinations of budgets and hyperparameters. This is akin to how classical UCB-E is often competitive with basic SR for appropriately chosen hyperparameters (Audibert et al., 2010) and motivates additional research into how model similarity can be effectively used by UCB algorithms. Our SyUCB-E baseline is a first step in this direction, as it consistently outperforms standard UCB-E, but the proof techniques from Theorem 5.1 are not directly applicable to SyUCB-E.

Second, despite its relatively weak average performance, we observe UCB-E-LRF (Zhou et al., 2025) performing very well on a small subset of benchmarks, even with minimal data. This motivates future work on designing more robust algorithms based on low-rank factorization or other imputation methods. Ideally, these algorithms could realize the occasional strong gains from LRF, while failing more gracefully in other cases and coming with theoretical guarantees.

Third, our work focuses on best model identification, but more general ranking objectives can be relevant in practice. A natural generalization is identifying or ranking the top mm models. We provide preliminary experiments in appendix H, observing that SySRs consistently outperforms SR. This indicates that synchronized evaluation might be useful for ranking models, more broadly. However, neither algorithm is explicitly designed for top-mm ranking. As such, we see synchronized versions of existing top-mm algorithms such as Successive Accepts and Rejects (SAR) (Bubeck et al., 2013) as a promising direction for future work.

8 Conclusion

In this work, we propose SySRs, a hyperparameter-free best-arm identification algorithm that exploits model similarity. We provide theoretical guarantees for SySRs that get stronger as the similarity among evaluated models increases. SySRs demonstrates strong empirical performance in both an average and a worst-case sense. Across a suite of 15 standard LLM benchmarks, SySRs reliably identifies the best model by evaluating at most 35%35\% of model/query pairs, greatly reducing the number of queries required for model selection. Beyond this, we believe that the structure of SySRs makes it well-suited for LLM inference: While UCB algorithms often choose to evaluate a different model at every step, SySRs evaluates each remaining model on a larger number of queries in each phase. This enables straightforward batching and can reduce overhead from reloading model weights when switching models.

Appendix A Detailed Analysis of the New Hardness Measure H3H_{3}

In this section, we characterize the regime of improvement, specifically determining the minimum level of correlation required for our correlation-aware complexity H3H_{3} to be strictly smaller than the standard H2H_{2}, and we state the formal version of the lower bound in Theorem 5.3.

Regime of Improvement.

Recall that both hardness measures are defined as maxima over the suboptimal arms:

H3=maxi∈{2,…,K}⁡i​H3,iandH2=maxi∈{2,…,K}⁡i​H2,iH_{3}\;=\;\max_{i\in\{2,\dots,K\}}iH_{3,i}\quad\text{and}\quad H_{2}\;=\;\max_{i\in\{2,\dots,K\}}iH_{2,i}

where we set H2,i≔Δi−2H_{2,i}\coloneqq\Delta_{i}^{-2}. While H2H_{2} is clearly unaffected by any correlation between the arms, expanding the variance in Equation 5 yields

H3,i\displaystyle H_{3,i} =2​V1+2​Vi+23​(1+Δi)​Δi−4​Cov⋆,iΔi2\displaystyle=\frac{2V_{1}+2V_{i}+\frac{2}{3}(1+\Delta_{i})\Delta_{i}-4\,\text{Cov}_{\star,i}}{\Delta_{i}^{2}}

where Vi=VarJ∼Unif​([L])⁡(S(i)​J)V_{i}=\operatorname{Var}_{J\sim\text{Unif}([L])}(S_{(i)J}) and Cov⋆,i=CovJ∼Unif​([L])​(Si⋆​J,S(i)​J)\mathrm{Cov}_{\star,i}=\mathrm{Cov}_{J\sim\text{Unif}([L])}(S_{i^{\star}J},S_{(i)J}). Thus, H3,iH_{3,i} strictly decreases with covariance for fixed marginal score distributions. We again express the (positive) covariance between the optimal arm i⋆i^{\star} and a suboptimal arm ii as a fraction of the maximal possible covariance for the mean arm scores:

θi=Cov⋆,iCovmax​(μ⋆,Δi)\theta_{i}\;=\;\frac{\mathrm{Cov}_{\star,i}}{\mathrm{Cov}_{\max}(\mu^{\star},\Delta_{i})}

where we used the shorthand notation Covmax​(μ⋆,Δi)=(μ⋆−Δi)​(1−μ⋆)\mathrm{Cov}_{\max}(\mu^{\star},\Delta_{i})=(\mu^{\star}-\Delta_{i})(1-\mu^{\star}) for the maximal achievable covariance between binary score distributions with means μ⋆\mu^{\star} and μ⋆−Δi\mu^{\star}-\Delta_{i}, and we assume that θi∈[0,1]\theta_{i}\in[0,1]. Since H3,iH_{3,i} decreases in θi\theta_{i} for fixed V1V_{1} and ViV_{i}, there exists a critical value θi⋆\theta_{i}^{\star} such that H3,i<H2,iH_{3,i}<H_{2,i} if and only if θi>θi⋆\theta_{i}>\theta_{i}^{\star}. The following proposition makes this statement rigorous.

Proposition A.1 (Correlation Threshold for Improvement).

For any arm i≠1i\neq 1, whenever the correlation coefficient θi\theta_{i} exceeds the threshold

θ⋆​(μ⋆,Δi):=−13​Δi2+Δi​μ⋆−13​Δi−(μ⋆)2+μ⋆−14(μ⋆−Δi)​(1−μ⋆),\theta^{\star}(\mu^{\star},\Delta_{i})\;:=\;\frac{-\frac{1}{3}\Delta_{i}^{2}+\Delta_{i}\mu^{\star}-\frac{1}{3}\Delta_{i}-(\mu^{\star})^{2}+\mu^{\star}-\frac{1}{4}}{(\mu^{\star}-\Delta_{i})(1-\mu^{\star})},

the correlation-aware hardness H3,iH_{3,i} is strictly smaller than the standard hardness H2,iH_{2,i}.

The proof is detailed in Appendix B. As a consequence of Proposition A.1, if every suboptimal arm satisfies the threshold condition, the correlation-aware hardness H3H_{3} is smaller than the standard hardness H2H_{2}. Moreover, we can derive Corollary 5.2.

The inequality H3<H2H_{3}<H_{2} implies a strictly tighter upper bound on the probability of error. Since the error rate scales as exp(−n/H)\exp(-n/H), even a constant factor reduction in the hardness parameter HH results in an exponential decay of the error probability for a fixed budget nn. Conversely, this means the algorithm requires significantly fewer samples to identify the best arm with high probability, when the correlation between models is sufficiently high (i.e. θi>θ⋆\theta_{i}>\theta^{\star}).

A Lower Bound.

To further justify the hardness measure H3H_{3}, we now show the formal version of Theorem 5.3. In the following result, we demonstrate that in a two-arm problem with correlated arms, in order to identify the better arm from nn i.i.d. paired score samples, any algorithm has to make an error that scales exactly as suggested by Theorem 5.1. Specifically, denote the function H3​(Δ,V)=(2​V+23​(1+Δ)​Δ)/Δ2H_{3}(\Delta,V)=(2V+\tfrac{2}{3}(1+\Delta)\Delta)/\Delta^{2}. Then we can show the following.

Theorem A.2.

For any Δ∈(0,1/2)\Delta\in(0,1/2) and s∈[Δ,1/2]s\in[\Delta,1/2], there exist distributions PP and QQ on {0,1}2\left\{0,1\right\}^{2} so that: First, 𝔼(X,Y)∼P[X−Y]=Δ\EE_{(X,Y)\sim P}\left[X-Y\right]=\Delta, that is, under PP, the best model is i⋆=1i^{\star}=1 and the gap to the second-best model is Δ\Delta, and 𝔼(X,Y)∼Q[X−Y]=−Δ\EE_{(X,Y)\sim Q}\left[X-Y\right]=-\Delta, that is, under QQ, the best model is i⋆=2i^{\star}=2 and the gap to the second-best model is Δ\Delta. Second, under both PP and QQ, the variance is V=s−Δ2V=s-\Delta^{2}, that is Var(X,Y)∼P⁡[X−Y]=Var(X,Y)∼Q⁡[X−Y]=V\operatorname{Var}_{(X,Y)\sim P}\left[X-Y\right]=\operatorname{Var}_{(X,Y)\sim Q}\left[X-Y\right]=V. And third, for any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and any algorithm I^:({0,1}2)n→{1,2}\widehat{I}:(\left\{0,1\right\}^{2})^{n}\to\left\{1,2\right\} that, based on nn i.i.d. samples 𝒟\mathcal{D} from PP or QQ, aims to identify the better model as I^​(𝒟)∈{1,2}\widehat{I}(\mathcal{D})\in\left\{1,2\right\}, incurs identification error at least 14​exp⁡(−11​nH3​(Δ,V))\frac{1}{4}\exp\left(-11\frac{n}{H_{3}(\Delta,V)}\right) on at least one of PP or QQ. That is, for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N},

infI^:({0,1}2)n→{1,2}max{ℙ𝒟∼Pn(I^(𝒟)≠1),ℙ𝒟∼Qn(I^(𝒟)≠2)}≥14exp(−11nH3​(Δ,V)).\inf_{\widehat{I}:(\left\{0,1\right\}^{2})^{n}\to\left\{1,2\right\}}\max\left\{\PP_{\mathcal{D}\sim P^{n}}\left(\widehat{I}(\mathcal{D})\neq 1\right),\PP_{\mathcal{D}\sim Q^{n}}\left(\widehat{I}(\mathcal{D})\neq 2\right)\right\}\geq\frac{1}{4}\exp\left(-11\frac{n}{H_{3}(\Delta,V)}\right).

Note that the gap Δ\Delta and variance VV here do not depend on the sample size n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. The proof is in Section B.4.

The key aspect of Theorem A.2 is that the difficulty of the problem is determined not only by the gap Δ\Delta, but also by the variance V=Var⁡[X−Y]V=\operatorname{Var}\left[X-Y\right], which captures the correlation structure between the two arms. Unlike classical bounds that depend only on marginal variances, here the hardness is expressed in terms of the variability of the difference X−YX-Y. This means that if the two arms are strongly positively correlated, then X−YX-Y has low variance and the problem becomes easier, whereas weak or negative correlation increases VV and thus the difficulty. The theorem shows that this is unavoidable and any algorithm using IID samples must incur an error that scales with H3​(Δ,V)H_{3}(\Delta,V). Exploiting correlation is not just beneficial but information-theoretically necessary for optimal performance, and matches Theorem 5.1.

Extending this bound to multiple arms is much more challenging, as while we can simulate nn arm pulls from nn paired evaluations of all KK arms, this comes at an overhead of KK model evaluations per arm pull; we leave the KK-arm case as interesting future work in the line of works such as Kaufmann et al. (2016); Carpentier and Locatelli (2016).

Appendix B Deferred Proofs

In this section we provide the deferred proofs for Theorems 5.1, A.2, A.1 and 5.2. To prove Theorem 5.1, we first provide two key technical concentration bounds.

B.1 Two Concentration Bounds

We use the following key lemma, a modified version of Bernstein’s inequality (Boucheron et al., 2003) that holds for sampling without replacement. Note that the following bound is slightly sharper than Proposition 1.4 in Bardenet and Maillard (2015) in the denominator of the exponential.

For a finite population indexed by {1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,N\} and a sample size 1≤n≤N1\leq n\leq N, we denote in the following section by

  • •

    πw\pi_{w}: an injection {1,…,n}→{1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{1,\ldots,N\} drawn uniformly at random (sampling without replacement);

  • •

    πr\pi_{r}: a function {1,…,n}→{1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{1,\ldots,N\} whose values are i.i.d. uniform on {1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,N\} (sampling with replacement).

Lemma B.1 (Bernstein bound for bounded variables without replacement).

Let 𝒵={ϕ1,…,ϕN}\mathcal{Z}=\{\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N}\} be a finite population of probability distributions such that for all ii, ϕi\phi_{i} takes values in [−M,M][-M,M], and such that these distributions verify

1N​∑i=1N𝔼Z∼ϕi​[Z]= 0,1N​∑i=1N𝔼Z∼ϕi​[Z2]=σ2.\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\phi_{i}}[Z]\;=\;0,\qquad\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\phi_{i}}[Z^{2}]\;=\;\sigma^{2}.

For any 1≤n≤N1\leq n\leq N, let (Zt)t=1n(Z_{t})_{t=1}^{n} be sampled by first drawing an injection πw\pi_{w} uniformly at random, and then drawing Zt∼ϕπw​(t)Z_{t}\sim\phi_{\pi_{w}(t)} independently for each tt. We define the empirical mean μ^Z,n:=1n​∑t=1nZt\widehat{\mu}_{Z,n}:=\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}Z_{t}. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, it holds that

ℙ⁡(μ^Z,n≥ε)≤exp⁡(−n​ε22​σ2+23​M​ε).\mathbb{P}\bigl(\widehat{\mu}_{Z,n}\geq\varepsilon\bigr)\;\leq\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}+\tfrac{2}{3}M\varepsilon}\right). (9)
Proof of Lemma B.1.

The proof follows by combining a standard moment generating function bound, e.g., from Boucheron et al. (2003), with Hoeffding’s reduction; see Hoeffding (1963, Theorem 4) or Bardenet and Maillard (2015, Lemma 1.1).

To develop the analysis, we begin by introducing a substitute (Z~t)t=1n(\widetilde{Z}_{t})_{t=1}^{n} of (Zt)t=1n(Z_{t})_{t=1}^{n}, sampled i.i.d. uniformly with replacement from the uniform mixture distribution ϕ¯=1N​∑i=1Nϕi\bar{\phi}=\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\phi_{i}, i.e. Z~t∼ϕπr​(t)\widetilde{Z}_{t}\sim\phi_{\pi_{r}(t)} conditionally on πr\pi_{r} . We have Z~t∼ϕ¯\widetilde{Z}_{t}\sim\bar{\phi}, yielding 𝔼⁡[Z~t]=0\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{Z}_{t}]=0, |Z~t|≤M|\widetilde{Z}_{t}|\leq M, and 𝔼⁡[Z~t 2]=σ2\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{Z}_{t}^{\,2}]=\sigma^{2}. Therefore, for every k≥2k\geq 2, it holds |Z~t|k≤Mk−2​Z~t 2|\widetilde{Z}_{t}|^{k}\leq M^{k-2}\,\widetilde{Z}_{t}^{\,2}, which implies that

𝔼⁡[|Z~t|k]≤σ2​Mk−2≤σ22​k!​(M3)k−2,∀k≥2.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,|\widetilde{Z}_{t}|^{k}\,\right]\;\leq\;\sigma^{2}M^{k-2}\;\leq\;\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\,k!\left(\frac{M}{3}\right)^{\!k-2},\qquad\forall k\geq 2. (10)

Now, fix λ>0\lambda>0 small enough such that u:=λ​M/3∈(0,1)u:=\lambda M/3\in(0,1). Using 𝔼⁡[Z~t]=0\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{Z}_{t}]=0 and inequality (10), we get that

𝔼⁡[eλ​Z~t]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda\widetilde{Z}_{t}}] =1+∑k≥2λkk!​𝔼​[Z~tk]≤ 1+∑k≥2λkk!​𝔼​[|Z~t|k]≤ 1+∑k≥2λk​σ22​(M3)k−2\displaystyle=1+\sum_{k\geq 2}\frac{\lambda^{k}}{k!}\,\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{Z}_{t}^{\,k}]\;\leq\;1+\sum_{k\geq 2}\frac{\lambda^{k}}{k!}\,\mathbb{E}[|\widetilde{Z}_{t}|^{k}]\;\leq\;1+\sum_{k\geq 2}\lambda^{k}\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\left(\frac{M}{3}\right)^{\!k-2}
=1+λ2​σ22​∑k≥2(λ​M3)k−2= 1+λ2​σ22⋅11−u≤exp⁡(λ2​σ22​(1−u)).\displaystyle=1+\frac{\lambda^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2}\sum_{k\geq 2}\!\left(\frac{\lambda M}{3}\right)^{\!k-2}\;=\;1+\frac{\lambda^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{1-u}\;\leq\;\exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2(1-u)}\right).

And by independence, we can use this bound to obtain

𝔼⁡[exp⁡(λ​∑t=1nZ~t)]≤exp⁡(n​σ2​λ22​(1−u)).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\!\Bigl(\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{n}\widetilde{Z}_{t}\Bigr)\right]\;\leq\;\exp\!\left(\frac{n\sigma^{2}\lambda^{2}}{2(1-u)}\right). (11)

We now come back to the sample without replacement employing Hoeffding’s reduction (Hoeffding, 1963). Defining φi​(λ):=log⁡𝔼Z∼ϕi​[eλ​Z]\varphi_{i}(\lambda):=\log\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\phi_{i}}\!\left[e^{\lambda Z}\right], conditional independence of (Zt)t=1n(Z_{t})_{t=1}^{n} given πw\pi_{w} yields

𝔼⁡[exp⁡(λ​∑t=1nZt)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\!\Bigl(\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{n}Z_{t}\Bigr)\right] =𝔼πw​[𝔼⁡[exp⁡(λ​∑t=1nZt)|πw]]=𝔼πw​[∏t=1n𝔼Z∼ϕπw​(t)​[eλ​Z]]\displaystyle\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{w}}\!\!\left[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\!\Bigl(\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{n}Z_{t}\Bigr)\,\Big|\,\pi_{w}\right]\right]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{w}}\!\!\left[\prod_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\phi_{\pi_{w}(t)}}\!\left[e^{\lambda Z}\right]\right]
=𝔼πw​[exp⁡(∑t=1nφπw​(t)​(λ))],\displaystyle\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{w}}\!\!\left[\exp\!\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{n}\varphi_{\pi_{w}(t)}(\lambda)\Bigr)\right],

and likewise 𝔼⁡[exp⁡(λ​∑tZ~t)]=𝔼πr​[exp⁡(∑tφπr​(t)​(λ))]\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\!\bigl(\lambda\sum_{t}\widetilde{Z}_{t}\bigr)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{r}}\!\!\left[\exp\!\bigl(\sum_{t}\varphi_{\pi_{r}(t)}(\lambda)\bigr)\right]. Since x↦exx\mapsto e^{x} is convex, sampling without replacement is dominated by sampling with replacement (Lemma 1.1 in Bardenet and Maillard (2015)) applied to the finite population {φi​(λ)}i=1N\{\varphi_{i}(\lambda)\}_{i=1}^{N}, meaning that

𝔼⁡[exp⁡(λ​∑t=1nZt)]=𝔼πw​[exp⁡(∑t=1nφπw​(t)​(λ))]≤𝔼πr​[exp⁡(∑t=1nφπr​(t)​(λ))]=𝔼⁡[exp⁡(λ​∑t=1nZ~t)]≤exp⁡(n​σ2​λ22​(1−u)),\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\!\Bigl(\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{n}Z_{t}\Bigr)\right]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{w}}\!\!\left[\exp\!\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{n}\varphi_{\pi_{w}(t)}(\lambda)\Bigr)\right]\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{r}}\!\!\left[\exp\!\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{n}\varphi_{\pi_{r}(t)}(\lambda)\Bigr)\right]\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\!\Bigl(\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{n}\widetilde{Z}_{t}\Bigr)\right]\;\leq\;\exp\!\left(\frac{n\sigma^{2}\lambda^{2}}{2(1-u)}\right),

where the last inequality is (11).

Hence for any s≥0s\geq 0, using Markov’s inequality with Sn=∑t=1nZtS_{n}=\sum_{t=1}^{n}Z_{t} yields

ℙ⁡(Sn≥n​σ2​λ2​(1−u)+s2λ)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\!\left(S_{n}\geq\frac{n\sigma^{2}\lambda}{2(1-u)}+\frac{s^{2}}{\lambda}\right) =ℙ⁡(eλ​Sn≥exp⁡(n​σ2​λ22​(1−u)+s2))≤e−s2.\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\!\left(e^{\lambda S_{n}}\geq\exp\!\Bigl(\frac{n\sigma^{2}\lambda^{2}}{2(1-u)}+s^{2}\Bigr)\right)\;\leq\;e^{-s^{2}}.

To conclude, fix ε>0\varepsilon>0 and choose u:=M​ε3​σ2+M​εu:=\frac{M\varepsilon}{3\sigma^{2}+M\varepsilon}, λ:=ε⁡(1−u)σ2\lambda:=\frac{\varepsilon(1-u)}{\sigma^{2}}, and s:=n​ε​1−u2​n​σ2s:=\frac{n\varepsilon\sqrt{1-u}}{\sqrt{2n\sigma^{2}}}. ℙ⁡(Sn≥n​ε)≤exp⁡(−n​ε22​σ2+23​M​ε).\mathbb{P}(S_{n}\geq n\varepsilon)\;\leq\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}+\tfrac{2}{3}M\varepsilon}\right).

which concludes the proof. ∎

Next, we can apply Lemma B.1 to derive the following bound for paired differences.

Lemma B.2 (Bernstein bound for paired differences).

B.2 Proof of Theorem 5.1

As in the standard analysis of Successive Rejects, we observe that at the start of phase kk, exactly k−1k-1 arms have been removed, and exactly K−(k−1)=K−k+1K-(k-1)=K-k+1 arms are still active. Therefore, at least one of the kk worst arms must still be in the active set. Therefore, if the optimal arm i⋆i^{\star} is dismissed at the end of phase kk, it must be that its empirical mean was smaller than the empirical mean of one of these surviving suboptimal arms. Formally, if at the end of phase kk the optimal arm is removed, there exists some i∈{K+1−k,…,K}i\in\{K+1-k,\ldots,K\} such that:

μ^i⋆,nk≤μ^(i),nk.\widehat{\mu}_{i^{\star},n_{k}}\;\leq\;\widehat{\mu}_{(i),n_{k}}.

By a union bound over all phases and all potential suboptimal arms in those phases, the error probability ene_{n} is bounded by:

en≤∑k=1K−1∑i=K+1−kKℙ⁡(μ^(i),nk≥μ^i⋆,nk).e_{n}\;\leq\;\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}\ \sum_{i=K+1-k}^{K}\mathbb{P}\!\left(\widehat{\mu}_{(i),n_{k}}\geq\widehat{\mu}_{i^{\star},n_{k}}\right). (13)

Fix a phase kk and an arm i∈{K+1−k,…,K}i\in\{K+1-k,\ldots,K\}. We observe stochastic rewards Xt∼ϕi⋆​πw​(t)X_{t}\sim\phi_{i^{\star}\pi_{w}(t)} and Yt∼ϕ(i)​πw​(t)Y_{t}\sim\phi_{(i)\pi_{w}(t)}, where πw\pi_{w} is the uniform injection drawn. This allows us to apply Lemma B.2 with Δ=Δi≥0\Delta=\Delta_{i}\geq 0 and σ2=V⋆,i\sigma^{2}=V_{\star,i}. Combined with substituting the arm-specific hardness measure we get

Appendix C Algorithms

C.1 Standard UCB-E Algorithm Without Replacement

This variant of UCB-E from Zhou et al. (2025) samples test instances without replacement per arm i.e each model is evaluated at most once on any given instance. This is a first step toward exploiting the correlation structure among LLMs, since it ensures that the empirical mean μ^i\widehat{\mu}_{i} aggregates information from NiN_{i} distinct tasks rather than potentially redundant ones, and it sets the stage for Synchronized UCB-E (Section C.3).

C.2 UCB-E-LRF

This adaptation of UCB-E relies on a low-rank approximation of the scoring matrix, fit from the partial set of observed evaluations. It yields both an imputed score matrix S^\widehat{S} and an associated uncertainty matrix RR that quantifies the confidence of each predicted entry. At each round, the algorithm selects the arm maximizing an index BiB_{i} that combines observed scores, imputed scores, and an uncertainty bonus, and then picks the unobserved instance with the highest uncertainty for that arm. We do not detail the estimation procedure for S^\widehat{S} and RR here and refer the reader to Zhou et al. (2025) for the full description.

C.3 Synchronized UCB-E

As a correlation-aware variant of the classical UCB-E algorithm (Audibert et al., 2010), we propose Synchronized UCB-E (also referred to as SyUCB-E). This algorithm leverages the correlation structure among models by ensuring that all arms are evaluated on the same sequence of test instances.

The key modification from standard UCB-E lies in the task selection strategy: instead of selecting test instances independently and uniformly at random for each arm, Synchronized UCB-E employs a global task schedule. Specifically, a random permutation σ\sigma of all test instances is drawn at the beginning. When an arm is selected for evaluation, it is evaluated on the test instance in this predetermined sequence corresponding to its current evaluation count. This approach ensures that arms with similar evaluation counts are evaluated on similar subsets of tasks, which can help to exploit the correlation between models’ performances on shared instances. Like the standard UCB-E, Synchronized UCB-E requires specification of an exploration parameter aa, which controls the exploration-exploitation trade-off through the upper confidence bound Ui=μ^i+aNiU_{i}=\widehat{\mu}_{i}+\sqrt{\frac{a}{N_{i}}}.

Appendix D Dataset Details

HELM Lite: We use 9 available tasks from the HELM Lite benchmark suite v1.10.0 (2024-11-05). The tasks and their subtasks are: commonsense (OpenBookQA), gsm (GSM8K), legalbench (5 subsets: abercrombie, corporate_lobbying, function_of_decision_section, international_citizenship_questions, proa), math (7 subjects at level 1 with chain-of-thought: algebra, counting_and_probability, geometry, intermediate_algebra, number_theory, prealgebra, precalculus), med_qa (MedQA), mmlu (5 subjects: abstract_algebra, college_chemistry, computer_security, econometrics, us_foreign_policy), narrative_qa (NarrativeQA), natural_qa (2 modes: closedbook, openbook), and wmt_14 (5 language pairs: cs-en, de-en, fr-en, hi-en, ru-en). For tasks with multiple subtasks, we compute model performance by averaging scores across all instances rather than averaging per-subtask averages. For each benchmark, we include all models (among a total of 83 models included in HELM) for which evaluation data on that benchmark were available for download in December 2025.

OpenLLM Leaderboard: We include 6 tasks from the OpenLLM Leaderboard. The tasks and their subtasks are: ifeval (instruction following evaluation), mmlu_pro (professional-level MMLU), arc_challenge (AI2 Reasoning Challenge), bbh (Big-Bench Hard with 24 subtasks including boolean_expressions, causal_judgement, date_understanding, disambiguation_qa, formal_fallacies, geometric_shapes, hyperbaton, logical_deduction variants, movie_recommendation, navigate, object_counting, penguins_in_a_table, reasoning_about_colored_objects, ruin_names, salient_translation_error_detection, snarks, sports_understanding, temporal_sequences, and tracking_shuffled_objects variants), gpqa (3 subsets: diamond, extended, main), and musr (3 subtasks: murder_mysteries, object_placements, team_allocation). For each benchmark we select all models from official providers (from a total of 470) for which complete evaluation data across all subtasks was available in December 2025.

Model Lists: Data from both sources includes hundreds of evaluated models; rather than listing all models in the paper, we provide a full list of evaluated models together with evaluation parameters and data sources at https://github.com/zifanlyu/llm-bandits-sysrs/blob/main/datasets/MODEL_CANDIDATES_AND_EVALUATION_PARAMETERS_BY_DATASET.md.

Appendix E Implementation Details

E.1 Budget Levels

We evaluate algorithm performance across a range of budget percentages relative to the total number of evaluations needed for exhaustive evaluation (i.e., K×LK\times L).

Budget Grid for SySRs, SyUCB-E, UCB-E, US and SyUS.

For all algorithms besides UCB-E-LRF and UCB-E-LRF(No Warm-up), we evaluate performance at every integer percentage 1%,2%,…,100%1\%,2\%,\ldots,100\%, augmented with sub-integer grid points {1.25%,1.5%,1.75%,2.5%,3.5%,4.5%,5.5%}\{1.25\%,1.5\%,1.75\%,2.5\%,3.5\%,4.5\%,5.5\%\} for finer resolution at low budgets, yielding 107 budget levels in total.

Budget Grid for UCB-E-LRF and UCB-E-LRF(No Warm-up).

UCB-E-LRF experiments are evaluated on a sparser grid of 38 budget levels: sub-integer steps {1.25%,1.5%,1.75%,2.5%,3.5%,4.5%,5.5%}\{1.25\%,1.5\%,1.75\%,2.5\%,3.5\%,4.5\%,5.5\%\}, every 1%1\% from 6%6\% to 10%10\%, every 2%2\% from 10%10\% to 20%20\%, and then every 5%5\% from 25%25\% to 100%100\%.

CB Computation.

For algorithms evaluated on the finer grid (all except UCB-E-LRF variants), the X% Confidence Budget (CB) is the minimum budget percentage at which the identification accuracy reaches X% and is maintained at all subsequent evaluated budget points. Since some experiments are evaluated on the sparser grid, we compute the CB of every UCB-E-LRF and UCB-E-LRF(No Warm-up) experiment by rounding down to the nearest evaluated budget point on the sparser grid. This approach provides a favorable comparison for UCB-E-LRF and UCB-E-LRF(No Warm-up), as it may underestimate the true CB (i.e., the actual threshold could occur between two evaluated points). Despite this favorable treatment of some baselines, SySRs still demonstrates superior performance across most datasets and thresholds (see Table 3).

E.2 Experimental Settings for SySRs, SyUCB-E, UCB-E, and SR

We perform 10001000 independent runs for each algorithm at each budget level to obtain robust estimates of the probability of identification. For UCB-E and SyUCB-E, we conduct a sensitivity analysis with respect to the exploration hyperparameter a∈{0.1,1.0,10.0,100.0}a\in\{0.1,1.0,10.0,100.0\}.

E.3 UCB-E-LRF Hyperparameters and Settings

For UCB-E-LRF, we use the implementation from the original authors’ codebase (Zhou et al., 2025). Based on their findings that the algorithm’s performance is not highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices, we adopt their default hyperparameter settings.

Due to the computational cost of the low-rank factorization approach, we run only 100100 independent runs (compared to 10001000 runs for other algorithms). We fix the rank parameter to r=1r=1 and use the following hyperparameters: ensemble size of 64, uncertainty scaling η=5.0\eta=5.0, dropout rate drop=0.05\text{drop}=0.05, ALS (Alternating Least Squares) regularization λ=0.1\lambda=0.1, 10 ALS iterations per update, batch size of 32 samples per UCB iteration, and warmup percentage T0=5%T_{0}=5\% of total matrix entries.

To evaluate the impact of the warmup phase, we also implement UCB-E-LRF(No Warm-up) with T0=0%T_{0}=0\% of total matrix entries while keeping all other hyperparameters unchanged.

E.4 Summary of Evaluated Algorithms and Their Characteristics.

We summarize the proposed and evaluated algorithms and their key characteristics in Table E.1, including their origin, whether they utilize synchronized evaluation, hyperparameter settings, and computational overhead per run.

Appendix G Subset Selection Experimental Details

We provide additional details on the subset selection experiments mentioned in the main paper, including the experimental setup and implementation details for each subset selection method.

G.1 Experimental Setup

Let 𝐒∈[0,1]K×L\mathbf{S}\in[0,1]^{K\times L} be the full score matrix over KK models and LL questions. The ground-truth best arm is i⋆∈arg⁡maxi⁡μii^{\star}\in\arg\max_{i}\mu_{i} where μi=1L​∑j=1LSi​j\mu_{i}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{j=1}^{L}S_{ij}. At budget fraction bb, the total query budget is ⌊b⋅K​L⌋\lfloor b\cdot KL\rfloor and the number of anchor questions is k=⌊b​L⌋k=\lfloor bL\rfloor. The subset selection methods are evaluated at the budget levels b∈{5%,10%,15%,20%,25%,30%,35%}b\in\{5\%,10\%,15\%,20\%,25\%,30\%,35\%\}. For each method and budget, we first select a subset of kk anchor questions using that method, then evaluate all KK models on the selected anchors, compute an estimate μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} for each model, and predict the best arm as ı^\hat{\imath}.

The clustering-based methods are each evaluated over 100 independent runs; the only source of randomness across runs is the clustering initialisation seed, while the score matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S} and all derived parameters (e.g., correlations, IRT parameters) are fixed. MetaBench is fully deterministic given 𝐒\mathbf{S}, so a single run suffices, and its best-arm identification rate is either 0 or 1 on a given dataset and budget.

G.2 Subset Selection via Anchor Point Weighted Score from Vivek et al. (2024)

We replicate the Anchor Point Weighted Score method from Vivek et al. (2024). First, we compute the inter-question Pearson correlation matrix C∈ℝL×LC\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L} with

Cj​i=corr(𝐒:j,𝐒:i),C_{ji}=\operatorname{corr}(\mathbf{S}_{:j},\,\mathbf{S}_{:i}),

and the distance matrix D=𝟏−CD=\mathbf{1}-C. We then run k-medoids on DD to obtain kk representative questions {q1,…,qk}\{q_{1},\ldots,q_{k}\}. Each question qq in the full benchmark is assigned to its most-correlated medoid,

aq=arg⁡maxl∈{1,…,k}⁡Cql,q,a_{q}=\arg\max_{l\in\{1,\dots,k\}}\;C_{q_{l},\,q},

and the weight of the anchor item qlq_{l} is set to the fractional cluster size of its assigned questions,

wl=|{q:aq=l}|L.w_{l}=\frac{|\{q:a_{q}=l\}|}{L}.

We then predict the score of model ii as the weighted average of its scores on the anchor questions,

μ^i=∑l=1kwl⋅Si​ql.\hat{\mu}_{i}=\sum_{l=1}^{k}w_{l}\cdot S_{iq_{l}}.

The only randomness across runs comes from the seed used by the k-medoids algorithm.

G.3 Subset Selection via K-means from Maia Polo et al. (2024)

We replicate two subset selection methods from Maia Polo et al. (2024) that differ only in how each question is embedded before clustering. Both methods run K-means with kk clusters on the question embeddings {xj}j=1L\{x_{j}\}_{j=1}^{L} and use the question nearest to each cluster centre as anchors,

ql⋆=arg⁡minq∈[L]⁡‖xq−cl‖2,q_{l}^{\star}=\arg\min_{q\in[L]}\;\|x_{q}-c_{l}\|_{2},

assign weight wl=|clusterl|/Lw_{l}=|\mathrm{cluster}_{l}|/L (fractional cluster size), and predict the score for model ii as

μ^i=∑l=1kwl⋅Si​ql⋆.\hat{\mu}_{i}=\sum_{l=1}^{k}w_{l}\cdot S_{iq_{l}^{\star}}.

Randomness across runs comes solely from the K-means initialisation seed.

IRT-based subset selection.

A multidimensional 2PL IRT model is fitted once to 𝐒\mathbf{S} and cached. The model assigns each question jj a discrimination vector αj∈ℝD−1\alpha_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{D-1} and scalar difficulty βj∈ℝ\beta_{j}\in\mathbb{R}, with item response probability

Pi​j=σ⁡(αj⊤​θi−βj),P_{ij}=\sigma\!\left(\alpha_{j}^{\top}\theta_{i}-\beta_{j}\right),

where θi∈ℝD−1\theta_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D-1} is the latent ability of model ii. The IRT is fitted with hierarchical priors via MAP estimation for 2000 epochs. Each question is embedded as xj=(αj,βj)∈ℝDx_{j}=(\alpha_{j},\,\beta_{j})\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. We evaluate D∈{2,5,10,15}D\in\{2,5,10,15\}, corresponding to D−1D-1 discrimination dimensions.

Correctness-based subset selection.

Each question jj is embedded directly as its score vector across all KK models,

xj=𝐒:j∈ℝK,x_{j}=\mathbf{S}_{:j}\in\mathbb{R}^{K},

i.e. the column of 𝐒\mathbf{S} recording each model’s binary score on question jj. No IRT fitting is required.

G.4 MetaBench from Kipnis et al. (2025)

MetaBench (Kipnis et al., 2025) selects a subset of kk questions via a Fisher-information quantile criterion on a fitted 2PL IRT model, then predicts each model’s full-bank mean score using a calibrated generalized additive model (GAM). The procedure is entirely deterministic given 𝐒\mathbf{S}.

Step 1: Fit a 2PL IRT model.

A 2PL IRT model is fitted to 𝐒\mathbf{S} with fixed initialisations, yielding discrimination αj∈ℝ\alpha_{j}\in\mathbb{R} and difficulty βj∈ℝ\beta_{j}\in\mathbb{R} for each question jj, and ability θi∈ℝ\theta_{i}\in\mathbb{R} for each model ii.

Step 2. Subset Selection based on Fisher Information

The KK fitted abilities are partitioned into kk equal-probability quantile bins ℬt={i:θ^i∈[τt,τt+1)}\mathcal{B}_{t}=\{i:\hat{\theta}_{i}\in[\tau_{t},\tau_{t+1})\}, t=1,…,kt=1,\ldots,k. For t=1,…,min⁡(k,K)t=1,\ldots,\min(k,K), the anchor for bin tt is the not-yet-selected question with the highest average Fisher information over models in that bin,

qt=arg⁡maxj∉Qt−1​1|ℬt|​∑i∈ℬtaj2​Pi​j​(1−Pi​j),q_{t}=\arg\max_{j\notin Q_{t-1}}\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{t}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}a_{j}^{2}\,P_{ij}(1-P_{ij}),

where Qt−1={q1,…,qt−1}Q_{t-1}=\{q_{1},\ldots,q_{t-1}\}. Any remaining slots (t>Kt>K, since each bin yields at most one distinct item) are filled by the question with the highest global average Fisher information:

qt=arg⁡maxj∉Qt−1​1K​∑i=1Kaj2​Pi​j​(1−Pi​j).q_{t}=\arg\max_{j\notin Q_{t-1}}\;\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}a_{j}^{2}\,P_{ij}(1-P_{ij}).

The final subset is Q∗={q1,…,qk}Q^{*}=\{q_{1},\ldots,q_{k}\}.

Step 3: Calibrate a GAM and predict.

A per-subset ability θ^iQ∗\hat{\theta}_{i}^{Q^{*}} is re-estimated on Q∗Q^{*} only. A two-term GAM

μ^i=f1​(θ^iQ∗)+f2​(S¯iQ∗)+c\hat{\mu}_{i}=f_{1}\!\bigl(\hat{\theta}_{i}^{Q^{*}}\bigr)+f_{2}\!\bigl(\bar{S}_{i}^{Q^{*}}\bigr)+c

is fitted by penalised least squares with the full-bank mean μi\mu_{i} as the response, where S¯iQ∗\bar{S}_{i}^{Q^{*}} is model ii’s mean score on Q∗Q^{*} and f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} are cubic spline smooths. The predicted best model is ı^=arg⁡maxi⁡μ^i\hat{\imath}=\arg\max_{i}\hat{\mu}_{i}.

G.5 Results and Comparison to SySRs

We fit all subset selection methods on the full matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}. There is no train/test split. This setup gives a large advantage to the subset selection methods, as only some entries of 𝐒\mathbf{S} would be known a priori in practice. Indeed, knowing the full matrix trivializes the model selection problem, as all models’ average performance would already be known with high precision. Despite this advantage, we find that for model selection, the subset selection methods still fail to match the performance of SySRs. Figure G.1 shows the mean identification error rate across all 15 datasets. In particular, the identification error rate of SySRs, using only 5% of the budget is roughly on par with the error rate of the best subset selection method using 30% of the budget. This is perhaps unsurprising, as subset selection methods are not built for model selection specifically, and our experimental setup still requires them to evaluate all models on the full subset selection. In principle, subset selection methods could be combined with the bandit approach, but this would forego theoretical guarantees for empirical gains that are relatively minor in many settings Yauney et al. (2026).

Appendix H Top-mm Ranking and Identification

We now extend the evaluation framework of Section 6 beyond best-arm identification to the top-mm identification and ranking problem, where the goal is to recover the set of the mm strongest models given a fixed budget.

H.1 Problem Formulation

Recall the score matrix 𝐒∈[0,1]K×L\mathbf{S}\in[0,1]^{K\times L} and mean performance μi=1L​∑j=1LSi​j\mu_{i}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{j=1}^{L}S_{ij}. Based on the mean performance on the benchmark, the models are ordered and indexed in decreasing order with μ(1)≥μ(2)≥⋯≥μ(K)\mu_{(1)}\geq\mu_{(2)}\geq\cdots\geq\mu_{(K)}, and we define the true top-mm set for a given m∈{1,…,K−1}m\in\{1,\dots,K-1\},

𝒯m⋆={(1),(2),…,(m)}.\mathcal{T}_{m}^{\star}\;=\;\bigl\{(1),\,(2),\,\dots,\,(m)\bigr\}.

An algorithm with budget nn produces a ranked list of mm models π^=(π1,π2,…,πm)\widehat{\pi}=(\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\dots,\pi_{m}), where πr\pi_{r} denotes the index of the model predicted to occupy rank rr, along with the corresponding predicted top-mm set 𝒯^m={π1,…,πm}\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{m}=\{\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{m}\}.

H.2 Ranking Procedure for Each Algorithm

Although the algorithms evaluated in Section 6 are designed to identify the best model, we introduce the following mechanisms to produce a ranked list for the models.

Mean-score Algorithms (US, SyUS, UCB-E, SyUCB-E).

For algorithms that do not perform explicit arm elimination, we rank all KK models according to their empirical mean score upon the completion of draws:

μ^i=1|𝒥i|​∑j∈𝒥iSi​j,\hat{\mu}_{i}\;=\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{J}_{i}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}}S_{ij},

where 𝒥i⊆𝒳\mathcal{J}_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{X} is the set of queries on which model ii was evaluated. Models are sorted in decreasing order of μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} to obtain π^\widehat{\pi}.

Elimination-Based Algorithms (SR, SySRs).

For algorithms that sequentially eliminate arms, we use the elimination order to assign ranks: the arm eliminated last is assigned rank 11 (best), the arm eliminated second-to-last is assigned rank 22, and so on. This is a natural byproduct of the algorithm’s execution and requires no additional computation.

H.3 Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate top-mm performance using three complementary metrics. As in Section 6, b=nKD×LDb=\frac{n}{K_{D}\times L_{D}} denotes the budget percentage used for evaluation. Our experiments use a uniform grid of budget percentages with step size 5%, from 0% to 100%.

Top-mm Identification Error Rate.

For a single run, an algorithm fails to identify the top-mm set if its predicted set differs from the true top-mm set:

𝟏[𝒯^m≠𝒯m⋆]∈{0,1}.\mathbf{1}\bigl[\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{m}\neq\mathcal{T}_{m}^{\star}\bigr]\;\in\{0,1\}.

For example, if the true top-3 set is {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\} and an algorithm predicts {2,1,3}\{2,1,3\}, the result is 00 (correct). If the algorithm instead predicts {1,2,4}\{1,2,4\}, the result is 11 (error). The top-mm identification error rate ϵb(m)=ℙ⁡(𝒯^m≠𝒯m⋆)\epsilon_{b}^{(m)}=\mathbb{P}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{m}\neq\mathcal{T}_{m}^{\star}) is the probability of this event, estimated by averaging the binary outcome over independent runs. At m=1m=1 this coincides with the standard budget-indexed error probability ϵb\epsilon_{b}.

Top-mm Ranking Error Rate.

We define the top-mm ranking error rate as 00 if and only if the predicted top-mm ranking exactly matches the true top-mm ranking, and 11 otherwise:

rb(m)=ℙ⁡((π1,…,πm)≠((1),…,(m))).r_{b}^{(m)}\;=\;\mathbb{P}\bigl((\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{m})\neq\bigl((1),\ldots,(m)\bigr)\bigr).

Since correct exact ranking implies correct top-mm set identification, we have rb(m)≥ϵb(m)r_{b}^{(m)}\geq\epsilon_{b}^{(m)}.

Top-mm per-rank error rate.

The top-mm per-rank error rate measures the expected fraction of incorrectly ranked models:

ρb(m)=𝔼[1m∑r=1m𝟏[πr≠(r)]].\rho_{b}^{(m)}\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{m}\sum_{r=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}\bigl[\pi_{r}\neq(r)\bigr]\right].

For a single run, 1m∑r=1m𝟏[πr≠(r)]∈[0,1]\frac{1}{m}\sum_{r=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}[\pi_{r}\neq(r)]\in[0,1] expresses the fraction of top-m positions rr for which the predicted rank-rr model does not coincide with the true rank-rr model; we obtain an estimate ρ^b(m)\hat{\rho}_{b}^{(m)} by averaging this quantity over independent runs.

Computation of Evaluation Metrics for Tied Models

Some of our datasets have multiple models tied for the same rank. In that case, we treat all produced rankings that are consistent with the tied ranking as correct. For example, if two models are tied for rank two, ranking either of these models at rank two or three is counted as correct. Formally, we consider all proper rankings that are consistent with the tied ranking and for each run we compute the error rates as the minimum error rate over all these rankings.

Top-mm Confidence Budget.

Analogously to the X% Confidence Budget (CB) defined in Section 6, we define the X% top-mm identification CB as the minimum budget percentage bD,m⋆b_{D,m}^{\star} such that the empirical top-mm identification error rate ϵ^b(m)\hat{\epsilon}_{b}^{(m)} is at most (100−X)%(100-X)\% for all evaluated budget percentages b≥bD,m⋆b\geq b_{D,m}^{\star}. The X% top-mm ranking-error CB and X% top-mm per-rank-error CB are defined analogously. As in the best-arm case, we report the worst-case (maximum) CB across the 15 benchmark datasets.

H.4 Results

We present the following observations from the error-rate and CB views of the performance of algorithms on the Top-mm identification and ranking problem.

H.4.1 Top-mm Error-rate curves

Figure H.1 reports ϵ^b(m)\hat{\epsilon}_{b}^{(m)} as a function of budget for m∈{3,5,10}m\in\{3,5,10\}, averaged across the 15 datasets, where lower curves indicate more sample-efficient recovery of the top-mm set. Figure H.2 shows the stricter ranking metric r^b(m)\hat{r}_{b}^{(m)}, which counts an error unless the full top-mm order is exactly correct. Figure H.3 provides the results for the alternative ranking metric per-rank accuracy error, which measures the fraction of rank positions assigned incorrectly.

There are similar trends across the results of the three metrics. SySRs is strongest for m=3m=3 in terms of worst-case performance, and on par with SyUCB-E in terms of average error rates. For m=5m=5, SySRs’ worst case performance remains best, but SyUCB-E performs better in terms of average error rate, for the right hyperparameters. For m=10m=10, this gap widens, and unsynchronized UCB-E starts to outperform SySRs in terms of worst case performance for larger target accuracies.
